blocks.text: 75. History and Basic Concepts of Evolution

segments.text: Evolutionary theory — the scientific framework explaining how species change over time and how the diversity of life arose — provides the essential unifying conceptual framework underlying much of the taxonomy, physiology, and ecology content addressed throughout this subject, and this topic traces its historical development and establishes its core concepts.
Pre-Darwinian ideas.

Before Charles Darwin’s work, various naturalists had proposed that species could change over time (contradicting the then-dominant view of species as fixed and unchanging since their original creation), including Jean-Baptiste Lamarck’s early 19th-century theory proposing that organisms could acquire beneficial characteristics during their own lifetime (through use or disuse of particular features) and directly pass these acquired characteristics on to their offspring — a mechanism now understood, based on modern genetic understanding (Topics 79–82), to be generally incorrect as a primary evolutionary mechanism (since heritable genetic material is not typically altered by an organism’s lifetime experiences in the direct, systematic way Lamarck’s theory proposed), though Lamarck’s broader proposal that species do change over time represented an important conceptual precursor to Darwin’s subsequent, more scientifically robust theory.
Darwin’s contribution.

Charles Darwin’s 1859 publication On the Origin of Species proposed natural selection (examined in detail in Topic 78) as the primary mechanism driving evolutionary change — the theory that heritable variation exists within populations, that this variation affects individual organisms’ relative survival and reproductive success, and that traits associated with greater survival and reproductive success will consequently become more common in subsequent generations, gradually altering a population’s characteristics over successive generations without requiring any deliberate direction or acquired-characteristic inheritance mechanism.
The modern evolutionary synthesis.

Darwin’s original theory, developed well before the molecular understanding of genetics and heredity established through the work discussed in Topics 68 and 79–82, was subsequently integrated with Mendelian genetics and, later, molecular genetic understanding during the mid-20th century “modern synthesis,” which provided the specific mechanistic explanation (mutation as the source of new heritable variation, Topic 73; Mendelian inheritance patterns explaining how this variation is passed to offspring, Topic 68) that Darwin’s original theory had lacked, producing the comprehensive, mechanistically well-supported evolutionary framework accepted within mainstream biological science today.
Core evolutionary concepts.

These include the basic requirement of heritable variation (a population must contain genetically-based variation in traits for natural selection to act upon, ultimately supplied by the mutation process discussed in Topic 73), differential survival and reproduction (individuals with certain trait variations must, on average, survive and reproduce more successfully than individuals with alternative trait variations, under the specific environmental conditions the population experiences), and the resulting change in trait frequency across successive generations — collectively defining evolution, at its most basic level, as a change in the heritable characteristics of a population over successive generations.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Lamarck’s early theory of acquired-characteristic inheritance is now understood to be generally incorrect, but represented an important conceptual precursor to Darwin’s subsequent theory of evolution by natural selection.
Darwin’s 1859 theory proposed natural selection — differential survival and reproduction based on heritable variation — as the primary evolutionary mechanism, without requiring deliberate direction.

The mid-20th century “modern synthesis” integrated Darwin’s theory with Mendelian and molecular genetics, providing the specific mechanistic explanation for heritable variation’s origin and inheritance that produces the comprehensive evolutionary framework accepted today.

segments.text: The origin and early evolution of life addresses how the very first living organisms arose from non-living chemical matter, and how the fundamental cellular characteristics distinguishing major groups of living organisms (including the plant kingdom addressed throughout this subject) subsequently evolved — representing an area characterised by somewhat greater scientific uncertainty than the well-established core mechanisms of evolution by natural selection (Topic 78), given the practical challenge of directly observing or definitively reconstructing events that occurred billions of years ago.
The chemical origin of life (abiogenesis).

Current scientific understanding proposes that life originated through a gradual chemical process on early Earth, in which simple organic (carbon-containing) molecules formed from even simpler inorganic starting materials (under early Earth’s specific atmospheric and environmental conditions, quite different from today’s oxygen-rich atmosphere), and these simple organic molecules subsequently combined and organised into progressively more complex structures, eventually giving rise to self-replicating molecular systems and, ultimately, the first simple cellular life forms — while the precise specific chemical pathway remains an area of active scientific research and some continuing uncertainty (given the practical difficulty of directly testing or observing processes that occurred so long ago under environmental conditions difficult to precisely recreate), the basic principle that life arose through a gradual chemical process from non-living matter, rather than requiring some entirely separate, non-chemical originating mechanism, is well supported by the convergent evidence discussed below.
Early cellular evolution: prokaryotes preceding eukaryotes.

The earliest life forms are understood to have been simple, relatively small, prokaryotic cells (cells lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound internal organelles, in contrast to the more structurally complex eukaryotic cells, including plant cells, discussed extensively in the Cytology section, Topics 62–67) — more structurally complex eukaryotic cells are understood to have evolved considerably later.
The endosymbiotic theory.

As introduced briefly in Topic 67’s ultrastructure discussion, the endosymbiotic theory proposes that key eukaryotic cell organelles — specifically chloroplasts and mitochondria — originated as formerly free-living prokaryotic organisms that were engulfed by, and eventually became permanently integrated within, an ancestral host cell, evolving over time from an initially separate, free-living organism into a permanently integrated cellular organelle. This theory is supported by several distinctive lines of evidence: both chloroplasts and mitochondria possess their own distinct DNA, structurally distinct from and organised differently than the cell’s main nuclear DNA; both organelles are enclosed by a double membrane (consistent with an original engulfment process, in which an outer membrane derived from the host cell’s own engulfing membrane would have enclosed the pre-existing single membrane of the originally free-living engulfed organism); and both organelles can self-replicate through a division process occurring somewhat independently of, though still coordinated with, the host cell’s own overall cell division cycle (Topic 62) — together, this evidence provides compelling, mutually reinforcing support for chloroplasts’ and mitochondria’s proposed evolutionary origin as formerly independent organisms.
Significance for understanding plant evolution.

This deep evolutionary history — the chemical origin of the first cellular life, and the subsequent endosymbiotic origin of the chloroplast, the organelle whose photosynthetic function (Topics 45–47) ultimately makes all subsequent plant life and, indeed, virtually all other life on Earth possible, given photosynthesis’s foundational role in global food webs (Topic 54) — provides essential deep evolutionary context for understanding the entire subsequent history of plant evolution traced throughout this subject, from algae (Topics 1–4) through the progressively more complex land plant groups discussed in Sections I through IV.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Current scientific understanding proposes life originated through a gradual chemical process (abiogenesis) from simple organic molecules under early Earth’s specific environmental conditions, though the precise chemical pathway remains an area of ongoing research.
The earliest life forms were simple prokaryotic cells, with more structurally complex eukaryotic cells (including plant cells) evolving considerably later.

The endosymbiotic theory, supported by distinctive DNA, double-membrane, and independent-replication evidence, proposes that chloroplasts and mitochondria originated as formerly free-living prokaryotic organisms engulfed by and integrated within an ancestral host cell.

segments.text: Convergent, divergent, and parallel evolution describe three distinct patterns by which evolutionary change can produce similarity or difference among species — understanding these distinct patterns is essential for correctly interpreting observed similarities and differences between species, directly relevant to the taxonomic classification challenges discussed in Topic 29, where distinguishing genuine shared ancestry from merely superficial similarity is a central concern.
Divergent evolution.

This describes the pattern in which related species, sharing a common evolutionary ancestor, become progressively more different from one another over evolutionary time, typically as a result of adapting to different environmental conditions or ecological niches following some form of separation (connecting directly to the allopatric speciation mechanism discussed in Topic 31) — divergent evolution is, in essence, the standard, expected pattern of evolutionary diversification from a common ancestor, and produces the branching, tree-like pattern of evolutionary relationship that phylogenetic classification (Topic 29) aims to accurately reconstruct and represent.
Convergent evolution.

This describes the notably different pattern in which unrelated or only distantly related species, not sharing a particularly recent common ancestor, independently evolve similar characteristics or adaptations, typically because they face similar environmental pressures or occupy similar ecological niches, despite their considerable underlying evolutionary distance — convergent evolution is of particular importance for taxonomic classification because it can produce misleading superficial similarity that might naively suggest close evolutionary relationship where genuine close relationship does not actually exist, directly explaining why modern phylogenetic classification increasingly relies on molecular genetic evidence (Topic 29) rather than morphological similarity alone, since molecular evidence is generally much less susceptible to this convergent evolution confound than superficial structural similarity is. A frequently cited example relevant to plant biology involves cactus-like succulent plant forms, which have evolved independently in several entirely distinct, only distantly related plant lineages in different arid regions of the world, converging on broadly similar water-storage and drought-adaptation strategies (including thick, water-storing tissue and reduced leaf surface area) in response to similarly harsh, water-scarce environmental conditions, despite these convergent succulent lineages not sharing a particularly close common ancestor.
Parallel evolution.

This describes a pattern somewhat intermediate between divergent and convergent evolution — related species (sharing a relatively more recent common ancestor than the distantly related species involved in typical convergent evolution cases) independently evolve similar adaptations following their initial divergence, typically because they face similar environmental pressures, but starting from a shared underlying genetic and developmental foundation inherited from their more recent common ancestor (in contrast to convergent evolution, where the independently evolving lineages start from a much more evolutionarily distant, dissimilar underlying genetic and developmental starting point).
Practical significance for interpreting plant characteristics.

Understanding these three distinct evolutionary patterns has direct practical significance for correctly interpreting observed plant characteristics and for constructing accurate taxonomic classifications — a researcher observing similar characteristics across different plant species must carefully consider whether that similarity most likely reflects genuine shared ancestry (divergent evolution from a common ancestor, with the similarity representing a retained ancestral characteristic) or independently evolved convergent/parallel adaptation to similar environmental pressures (in which case the similarity, however striking, does not necessarily indicate particularly close evolutionary relationship) — a distinction of direct relevance to the chemotaxonomy discussion in Topic 33, where convergently evolved similar defensive secondary metabolite compounds across unrelated plant lineages represent exactly this kind of potentially taxonomically misleading convergent similarity.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Divergent evolution describes related species from a common ancestor becoming progressively more different over time, representing the standard, expected pattern of evolutionary diversification.

Convergent evolution describes unrelated or distantly related species independently evolving similar characteristics due to similar environmental pressures, potentially producing misleading superficial similarity that does not indicate close relationship — as seen in independently evolved succulent, cactus-like plant forms across different lineages.

Parallel evolution describes related species (sharing a more recent common ancestor than typical convergent cases) independently evolving similar adaptations from a shared genetic starting point, representing a pattern intermediate between divergent and convergent evolution.

segments.text: Natural selection, introduced in Topic 75 as Darwin’s central proposed evolutionary mechanism, represents the process by which heritable traits that enhance an organism’s survival and reproductive success within a given environment become progressively more common within a population over successive generations — this topic examines the specific requirements and mechanisms of natural selection in more detail.
Requirements for natural selection to operate.
Three fundamental conditions must be met for natural selection to produce evolutionary change within a population:
heritable variation

(individuals within the population must vary in some trait, and this variation must have at least a partly genetic basis capable of being passed to offspring, ultimately supplied by the mutation process discussed in Topic 73, and reshuffled each generation through the Mendelian inheritance mechanisms discussed in Topic 68);
differential fitness

(this trait variation must be associated with differences in survival and/or reproductive success — individuals with certain trait variants must, on average, survive to reproductive age and/or produce more successful offspring than individuals with alternative trait variants, under the specific environmental conditions the population currently experiences); and
inheritance

(offspring must tend to resemble their parents for the trait in question, ensuring that traits associated with higher relative fitness are more likely to be passed on and to become correspondingly more common in the subsequent generation) — when all three conditions are met, the trait variants associated with higher relative fitness will, on average, become progressively more common within the population over successive generations, constituting evolutionary change by natural selection.
Types of selection patterns.
Directional selection

favours one extreme of a trait’s range of variation over the alternative extreme (and over intermediate values), progressively shifting the population’s average trait value in that favoured direction over successive generations — a pattern of direct relevance to artificial selection in crop breeding (Agriculture & Forestry subject), where breeders deliberately apply strong directional selection pressure favouring specific desired traits (such as higher yield or specific disease resistance).
Stabilising selection

favours intermediate trait values over both extremes, tending to reduce a population’s overall trait variation around an already well-adapted intermediate optimum, rather than shifting the population average in either direction.
Disruptive selection

favours both extremes of a trait’s range over intermediate values, potentially, in some cases, contributing to eventual population divergence and even speciation (Topic 31) if the favoured extreme trait values become associated with sufficient reproductive isolation between the two diverging extreme-trait subpopulations.
Adaptation as natural selection’s characteristic outcome.

Sustained natural selection, operating consistently over many successive generations, produces adaptation — the progressive evolutionary refinement of a population’s characteristics to better suit its specific environmental conditions and ecological niche, explaining the generally excellent apparent “fit” observed between most organisms’ characteristics and the specific environmental challenges they face (such as the drought-adaptation strategies convergently evolved by succulent plants discussed in Topic 77, or the salt-tolerance mechanisms evolved by halophyte plants discussed in Topic 59) — though it is important to recognise that natural selection acts only upon existing heritable variation already present within a population (it cannot directly generate specifically needed new variation on demand, but can only select among whatever variation the ongoing mutation process happens to have already supplied), and that natural selection optimises for reproductive success under current environmental conditions specifically, not for any independent notion of an organism’s overall “perfection,” meaning adaptations that were advantageous under past environmental conditions can become disadvantageous, or even actively maladaptive, if environmental conditions subsequently change — directly relevant to understanding species’ vulnerability to rapid environmental change, including the ongoing climate change discussed extensively in the Environmental Sciences subject, since evolutionary adaptation through natural selection generally requires many generations to produce significant change, a timescale that may not keep pace with sufficiently rapid environmental change.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Natural selection requires heritable variation, differential fitness associated with that variation, and inheritance of the trait to offspring; when all three conditions are met, favoured trait variants become progressively more common over successive generations.

Directional selection shifts a population’s average trait value toward one extreme (relevant to artificial crop breeding selection); stabilising selection favours intermediate values, reducing variation; disruptive selection favours both extremes, potentially contributing to speciation.

Sustained natural selection produces adaptation to current environmental conditions specifically, but cannot generate needed variation on demand and can leave populations vulnerable when environmental change occurs faster than evolutionary adaptation can keep pace, directly relevant to species vulnerability under rapid climate change.
